keyTakeaways: Pack light—aim for under 15kg of luggage for a week-long tour and use the 'remove a third' rule after laying everything out
Always pack in waterproof dry bags inside your main luggage, regardless of waterproofing claims—British weather will find a way in
Distribute weight low and centred on the bike with heavy items in lower panniers and lighter items higher up for better handling
Use an accessibility hierarchy—frequently needed items like waterproofs go on top, tools and spare parts at the bottom
Test your fully-loaded setup with a 50-mile shake-down ride before your actual tour to identify problems early
Pack layers for clothing rather than bulk—British weather can change drastically within a single day's riding

faq.q: How much luggage capacity do I need for a week-long motorcycle tour?
faq.a: For a week-long tour staying in accommodation, 40-60 litres total capacity works well—typically achieved with panniers or a combination of tail bag and tank bag. If camping, you'll need 60-80 litres to accommodate tent and sleeping gear.

faq.q: Should I choose soft or hard luggage for my first touring trip?
faq.a: Soft luggage is better for beginners—it's cheaper, lighter, and more forgiving when you overpack. Start with a quality tail bag and tank bag combination, then upgrade to hard luggage if you find yourself touring regularly.

faq.q: How do I pack for unpredictable British weather on a motorcycle tour?
faq.a: Use a layering system with thermal base layers, a mid-layer fleece, and waterproof over-trousers. Pack everything in dry bags inside your luggage and keep waterproofs accessible at the top of your panniers for quick access when weather changes.

faq.q: What tools should I carry on a UK motorcycle tour?
faq.a: Carry basic Allen keys, screwdrivers, pliers, cable ties, a puncture repair kit with tyre plugs, chain lube, spare bulbs and fuses, and duct tape. This covers most roadside issues without carrying a full workshop.

faq.q: How should I distribute weight on my motorcycle when touring?
faq.a: Place heavy items low and close to the bike's centre of gravity in the bottom of panniers. Keep weight balanced side-to-side and avoid overloading tank bags. Adjust tyre pressures and suspension preload according to your bike's manual for loaded riding.

faq.q: Do I need to adjust my bike before a loaded touring trip?
faq.a: Yes—increase tyre pressures according to your manual's loaded specifications, adjust suspension preload if possible, and do a test ride with full luggage to check handling. Also ensure your chain is clean and properly lubed before departure.

Motorcycle Touring Packing: Everything I've Learned on British Roads

I've been there—standing in my garage at 5am, bike loaded like a pack mule, wondering if I've forgotten something crucial. That first touring trip to Scotland taught me more about packing than any article ever could, but I wish someone had given me the straight truth before I set off. So here's what I know now, after thousands of miles exploring Britain's best roads.

Packing for a motorcycle tour isn't like throwing stuff in a car boot. Every item needs to earn its place, and the difference between a brilliant trip and a miserable one often comes down to what you've brought and how you've packed it. Let me walk you through exactly how I approach it these days.

The Golden Rule: Pack Light, Pack Right

I learned this the hard way on the NC500. I'd packed for every possible scenario, and by day three my bike was handling like a shopping trolley with a wonky wheel. The truth? You need less than you think, especially if you're staying in B&Bs or hotels.

Here's my rule: lay everything out that you think you need, then remove a third of it. Sounds brutal, but it works. Weight affects everything—braking, cornering, fuel consumption, and rider fatigue. I aim to keep my luggage weight under 15kg for a week-long tour, and I've managed trips with even less.

Understanding Your Luggage Options

Before we talk about what goes in your bags, let's discuss the bags themselves. I've used everything from bungee-corded sports bags (don't do this) to full pannier systems, and each has its place.

Soft luggage is brilliant for beginners. It's cheaper, lighter, and more forgiving when you inevitably pack too much. I started with a decent tail bag and tank bag combo, which served me perfectly for weekend trips across the Lake District and Wales. The key is waterproofing—even "waterproof" luggage can let water in during a proper British downpour. I always use dry bags inside my main luggage now.

Hard luggage offers better security and weather protection, but it's pricier and adds weight even when empty. If you're planning regular tours or heading up to the Highlands where weather changes by the minute, it's worth considering. Check out the range at SportsBikeShop—they've got options for every budget and bike type.

The Essential Packing List for British Touring

Right, let's get specific. This is what actually makes it into my luggage for a typical week-long British tour.

Clothing: Layers Are Your Best Mate

British weather is properly schizophrenic. I've ridden through sunshine, rain, and near-freezing conditions all in one day on the A537 Cat and Fiddle. Your clothing strategy needs to handle this.

  • Base layers: Two sets of thermal or moisture-wicking base layers. One worn, one packed. They dry overnight in most accommodation.
  • Mid layers: A fleece or thin down jacket that compresses small. I wear mine under my jacket on cold mornings in the Pennines.
  • Riding jeans or trousers: Two pairs maximum. One for riding, one for evenings. Modern riding jeans look normal enough for dinner.
  • Socks and underwear: Three or four sets. Quick-dry technical fabrics are worth every penny.
  • Casual top: One decent shirt or jumper for evenings. Most touring riders spend evenings in riding gear anyway.
  • Waterproofs: Even if your jacket has a waterproof liner, pack over-trousers. Scottish rain laughs at "waterproof" claims.

I use compression bags for clothes now. They're cheap, halve the space needed, and keep things organised. One bag for clean, one for dirty works perfectly.

Riding Gear Essentials

Beyond your main jacket and trousers, these smaller items make the difference:

  • Neck warmer or balaclava: Spring mornings on the Island to Highlands route can be bitter. This tiny item prevents misery.
  • Spare gloves: Lightweight summer gloves that pack flat. When your winter gloves are soaked after riding through the Trossachs in the rain, you'll thank me.
  • Visor anti-fog: Pinlock inserts are standard now, but I carry Foggy visor treatment as backup. British mist is relentless.
  • Buff or thin scarf: Multiple uses—sun protection, extra warmth, emergency oil rag.

Tools and Bike Kit

I'm not suggesting you pack a full workshop, but basic preparedness prevents disasters. This lot lives in my panniers permanently:

  • Basic tool kit: Most bikes come with one. If not, get Allen keys, screwdrivers, pliers, and cable ties.
  • Puncture repair kit: Including tyre plugs, CO2 canisters, and a compact pump. Used mine twice in the Highlands where mobile coverage was non-existent.
  • Chain lube and cleaner: 500 miles of wet Welsh roads will trash your chain. Clean and lube every few days.
  • Spare bulbs and fuses: Legal requirement in some countries, and sensible everywhere. Takes minimal space.
  • Bungee cords and rok straps: For securing odd items or emergency repairs. Always useful.
  • Duct tape: Wrap some around a pencil. Fixes everything temporarily.

The best packing system is one you can live with every day on the road. If accessing your waterproofs means unpacking everything, you won't bother until you're already soaked.

Electronics and Documents

Modern touring means staying connected, whether for navigation, accommodation booking, or just sharing photos from Applecross with mates back home.

  • Phone and charger: Obvious, but get a proper weatherproof mount and USB charging socket fitted to your bike.
  • Portable battery pack: For camping or when your accommodation has one socket hidden behind furniture.
  • Documents: Driving licence, insurance, breakdown cover details, and V5C if heading abroad. I photograph everything and keep digital copies too.
  • Camera: Your phone is probably fine, but if you're a photography enthusiast, a small action camera works brilliantly. The roads around the North Coast deserve proper documentation.

Packing Strategy: Where Everything Goes

Right, you've got your kit sorted. Now let's talk about actually packing the damn thing. Poor weight distribution turns your bike into a handful, especially in crosswinds on exposed coastal roads.

Weight Distribution Principles

Heavy items go low and close to the bike's centre of gravity. I pack my toolkit, chain lube, and any substantial items in panniers as low as possible. Light, bulky items like clothing go higher in panniers or in a top box.

Keep weight balanced side-to-side. If one pannier feels noticeably heavier, redistribute. I once rode 200 miles with uneven panniers and my back knew about it for days afterward.

Tank bags are perfect for items you need frequently—wallet, phone, snacks, maps. Keep the weight reasonable though; too much affects steering feel.

The Accessibility Hierarchy

Pack in layers based on how often you'll need things. This seems obvious until you're standing in a car park needing your waterproofs, which are buried under three days of clothes at the bottom of your pannier.

My system:

  • Tank bag: Phone, wallet, snacks, maps, visor cleaner, this morning's route notes from route builder.
  • Top of panniers: Waterproof jacket and trousers, spare gloves, anything I might need during riding.
  • Middle of panniers: Daily clothes, toiletries, evening wear.
  • Bottom of panniers: Tools, spare parts, items I won't need unless something goes wrong.
  • Tail bag: Extra layer clothing, camping gear if applicable, items needed at destination but not en route.

Waterproofing Everything

I cannot stress this enough: assume everything will get wet. I've had water seep into "waterproof" panniers, tank bags with "weather-resistant" zips, and supposedly sealed top boxes. British weather finds a way.

My approach now: everything goes in dry bags or ziplock bags first, then into main luggage. Electronics get double-bagged. Documents go in a waterproof document holder. This saved my arse when a pannier seal failed during a deluge near Fort William.

Category-Specific Packing Tips

Toiletries and Personal Items

Keep it minimal. Small travel-sized everything, and remember most accommodation provides basics. I pack:

  • Travel toothbrush and small toothpaste
  • Small soap bar (multipurpose—body, hands, emergency clothes wash)
  • Deodorant stick (aerosols take up space)
  • Sunscreen—yes, even in Britain. Sunburn at 60mph is miserable.
  • Basic first aid: plasters, painkillers, antihistamines, any personal medications
  • Earplugs if you're sensitive to noise or snoring roommates

Food and Hydration

A hydration pack or water bottles in bike mounts are essential. Dehydration kills concentration, and finding water on remote Highland roads isn't always easy. I aim to drink every hour when riding.

Pack energy bars or trail mix for long stretches. The A82 along Loch Lomond is stunning but services are spread out. Having snacks prevents making poor decisions when blood sugar drops.

Camping vs Accommodation Touring

If you're camping, obviously you need a tent, sleeping bag, and mat. This changes your packing completely. I'd suggest starting with accommodation touring to learn the basics, then progressing to camping once you've got your system sorted.

For camping tours, every gram counts even more. Invest in lightweight camping gear designed for cycle touring—it's expensive but genuinely lighter and more compact. My current camping setup adds about 5kg to my load.

Common Packing Mistakes I've Made (So You Don't Have To)

Let me save you some grief. These are mistakes that cost me comfort, money, or both:

  • Overpacking clothes: You'll wear the same riding jeans all week. Accept it.
  • Forgetting plug adaptors: Not an issue in Britain, but mentions it because Scottish Highland accommodation sometimes has older sockets.
  • Not securing luggage properly: Check straps and mounts daily. I lost a pannier strap on the A9 and only noticed at the next services. Lucky it stayed on.
  • Packing items you "might" need: If you haven't used it on previous trips, leave it home.
  • Ignoring weather forecasts: Check before you leave and pack accordingly. A week in the Highlands in June can mean anything from 25°C sunshine to 8°C rain.
  • Not testing your setup: Pack everything and ride 50 miles before your tour. You'll discover problems in your driveway area, not halfway to Skye.

Pre-Departure Checklist

Before you roll out of your garage, run through this. I use the packing checklist tool now which customises based on trip length and type, but here are the essentials:

  • All luggage secure and weight distributed evenly
  • Tyre pressures adjusted for load (check your manual—loaded touring needs higher pressure)
  • Suspension preload adjusted if possible
  • Chain clean and lubed
  • All lights working
  • Phone mounted and charged
  • Route loaded in GPS or noted
  • Accommodation booked (or wild camping spots researched)
  • Breakdown cover active and number saved
  • Someone knows your rough route and expected arrival

Final Thoughts From the Road

Packing for motorcycle touring is an evolving skill. Your first tour won't be perfect, and that's fine. I'm still tweaking my system after years of touring Britain's best roads. The key is starting with the basics, learning what works for you, and refining from there.

Remember that the point of touring isn't having the perfect packing system—it's experiencing incredible roads, stunning scenery, and the freedom that only comes from two wheels. Whether you're heading up to tackle the NC500 or exploring Welsh mountain passes, getting out there matters more than having everything perfectly optimised.

Start with your first weekend tour. Pack what seems sensible using these guidelines. Make notes about what you used, what you didn't, and what you wished you'd brought. Build from there. Every tour teaches you something new about your needs and preferences.

Now stop reading, start packing, and get out there. Britain's roads are waiting, and they're absolutely brilliant.
